correctness.summary: Modular exponentiation does plain long multiplication (res*a%mod and a*a%mod) without overflow-safe multiplication. For any modulus larger than floor(sqrt(long.MaxValue)) = 3037000499, the intermediate product a*a (with a up to mod-1) overflows signed 64-bit, wrapping to a negative/garbage value and producing a wrong result.
correctness.triggeringInput: Run(a=3999999999, e=2, mod=4000000000): a%=mod -> 3999999999; a*a = 15999999992000000001 overflows long.MaxValue (9223372036854775807), wrapping negative; the returned value does not equal (3999999999^2) mod 4000000000.
correctness.rootCause: Line 11 computes 'res = res * a % mod' and 'a = a * a % mod' directly in long arithmetic. With mod > sqrt(long.MaxValue) ~ 3.037e9, operands < mod can have products exceeding long range, so the multiply overflows before the % mod is applied.
correctness.suggestedFix: Route the multiplications through SafeMulMod.Run (after that routine itself is fixed) instead of raw '* % mod', e.g. res = SafeMulMod.Run(res, a, mod); a = SafeMulMod.Run(a, a, mod); or use Int128/UInt128 for the product.

correctness.summary: The large-modulus path (mod > int.MaxValue) reduces a*b via repeated doubling/addition using SafeAdd, which computes 'a + b' in plain long arithmetic. When the modulus exceeds long.MaxValue/2 (~4.61e18), operands a,b in [0,mod) can sum to more than long.MaxValue, overflowing to a negative value and corrupting the result. The routine is named 'Safe' but is not safe for the upper half of the valid long modulus range.
correctness.triggeringInput: Run(a=mod-1, b=mod-1, mod=(1L<<62)+5 = 4611686018427387909): inside the doubling loop SafeAdd(a,a,mod) computes (4611686018427387908 + 4611686018427387908) = 9223372036854775816 > long.MaxValue (9223372036854775807), overflowing to a negative number; result is wrong.
correctness.rootCause: Line 96 'long res = a + b; return res >= mod ? res - mod : res;' assumes a+b does not overflow long. That holds only when mod <= long.MaxValue/2. For mod in (long.MaxValue/2, long.MaxValue], a+b can overflow signed 64-bit before the comparison, so the conditional subtraction operates on a wrapped negative value.
correctness.suggestedFix: Detect overflow before subtracting: 'ulong s = (ulong)a + (ulong)b; if (s >= (ulong)mod) s -= (ulong)mod; return (long)s;' (unsigned sum cannot overflow since a,b < mod <= long.MaxValue, and a+b < 2*long.MaxValue < ulong.MaxValue), or use Int128.

perf.summary: IntegerSqrt.Run is called twice for the same x, doubling a ~31-iteration binary search with two mid*mid multiplies per iteration.
perf.currentCost: Two full IntegerSqrt binary searches (each ~31 loop iterations, each with a 64-bit multiply and compare) plus one final multiply. The square root is recomputed from scratch a second time even though it is identical.
perf.proposedChange: Compute the root once: long s = IntegerSqrt.Run(x); return x >= 0 && s * s == x; (x>=0 is already guaranteed inside IntegerSqrt which returns -1 for negatives, so the cheap fix is `long s = IntegerSqrt.Run(x); return s >= 0 && s * s == x;`). For x<0, IntegerSqrt returns -1, and (-1)*(-1)==1 != x for negative x, so the s>=0 guard preserves correctness while removing the second call.
perf.rationale: Halves the work of the dominant cost (the binary search). Caching the result removes ~31 iterations and ~31 multiplies plus the redundant comparison setup.
perf.risk: Must keep the x>=0 / s>=0 guard. IntegerSqrt.Run(x) returns -1 for x<0; using s = -1 then `s>=0` correctly yields false, identical to the original x>=0 check. No overflow concern: s <= 3037000499 so s*s fits in long without overflow for valid inputs (same as original).

perf.summary: Recomputes floor via FloorLog2 then separately tests power-of-two; the power-of-two test re-derives information already implied, but more importantly the call is fine — the real micro-win is ordering the cheap mask test first.
perf.currentCost: FloorLog2 (a ~6-branch cascade) always runs, then `(x & (x-1)) == 0` runs. For exact powers of two the +1 is skipped, but FloorLog2's full cascade still executes.
perf.proposedChange: Leave FloorLog2 (needed for the magnitude) but compute the power-of-two predicate before/in parallel as a branchless add: `int floor = FloorLog2.Run(x); return floor + (((x & (x - 1)) != 0) ? 1 : 0);` which is what it already does — this is essentially optimal. The only genuine improvement is marking FloorLog2 and CeilLog2 for inlining (already done). No change recommended beyond confirming the predicate increment is branchless.
perf.rationale: Branchless increment avoids a mispredict on the boundary between exact and non-exact powers.
perf.risk: None; arithmetic identical. Low impact — listed only for completeness; can be skipped.

perf.summary: These hot leaf methods lack [MethodImpl(AggressiveInlining)] while their tiny siblings (NormalizeModulo, Minimize, etc.) have it; inlining FastPow/SafeMulMod into callers exposes the modulus to constant-folding when mod is a compile-time constant.
perf.currentCost: Each call is a real function-call boundary (stack setup, no cross-procedure constant propagation). When `mod` is a literal at the call site, Burst/LLVM cannot strength-reduce the `% mod` into a multiply-shift magic-number division unless the body is inlined or mod is visible.
perf.proposedChange: Add [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] to FastPow.Run, IntegerSqrt.Run, IntegerCbrt.Run, NthRoot.Run (and its private CanMultiply), SafeMulMod.Run and SafeAdd. For the unrolled bit-twiddlers NextPowerOfTwo.Run (sibling PrevPowerOfTwo already has it) add it too for consistency and call-site folding.
perf.rationale: Inlining small/medium hot math routines lets LLVM constant-fold known moduli into magic-number division (replacing a 20-40 cycle DIV with a multiply+shift), removes call overhead in inner loops, and keeps values in registers across the boundary.
perf.risk: Inlining larger bodies (the while-loop reductions) increases code size; on mobile I-cache this is a tradeoff. AggressiveInlining is a hint Burst may decline for large bodies, so semantics are unaffected. The main, safe, high-value targets are NextPowerOfTwo (currently missing, sibling has it) and the leaf SafeAdd; the loop-bodies are optional.

perf.summary: CanMultiply recomputes `x / mid` (a division) inside its loop guard each iteration of the binary search, and binary-search hi bound `1L << (62/n + 1)` plus per-step overflow guard are heavier than needed for small n.
perf.currentCost: For each binary-search step (~62/n steps), CanMultiply loops up to n times doing `x / mid` (a divide) per iteration to avoid overflow. That is n divides per probe, O(n log range) divides total.
perf.proposedChange: Hoist the divisor-independent part where possible and special-case n==2 to delegate to IntegerSqrt.Run and n could fall through for n>=64 (where hi collapses to 1) early: `if (n >= 63) return x >= 1 ? 1 : 0;` Also for n==2 call IntegerSqrt directly to reuse its tighter 31-step search without the per-iteration division of CanMultiply. Keep the overflow-safe `p > x / mid` guard only for the general path.
perf.rationale: Delegating n==2 to IntegerSqrt removes the n-divides-per-probe overhead for the most common non-trivial root; the n>=63 short-circuit avoids a binary search whose answer is always 0 or 1.
perf.risk: Must match boundary results exactly. IntegerSqrt.Run returns floor(sqrt(x)) which equals NthRoot for n==2 for all x>=0 — verify both return the same for x==0 and perfect squares (they do). The n>=63 case: 2^63 overflows long, so any x>=1 has integer 63rd root >= 1 but < 2; floor is 1 for x>=1, 0 for x==0 — matches `x>=1?1:0`. Confirm 62/n+1 shift bound is unaffected for the remaining range.
